mcqs.question: If your application creates 50 user-level threads and none of them ever call a blocking system call, what does the OS scheduler see?
options: 50 independent schedulable entities, since the kernel tracks every thread you create
One process (with however many kernel threads the model maps it to), because pure user-level threads are invisible to the kernel scheduler
50 separate processes, since each thread runs as its own PID
Nothing — the OS refuses to run a process using user-level threads
mcqs.explanation: User-level threads are managed entirely by a userspace library; the kernel has no visibility into them and only sees whatever kernel-level entity (or entities) they're multiplexed onto. It doesn't see 50 separate schedulable things, and nothing about this setup is illegal or refused.

mcqs.question: Why is creating a kernel-level thread slower than creating a pure user-level thread, but still much cheaper than creating a whole new process?
options: It's actually the same cost as creating a process — the numbers only look different due to measurement noise
It goes through the kernel (unlike a user-level thread), which costs a syscall, but it reuses the process's existing address space instead of building a new one (unlike a process)
Kernel threads require allocating an entirely new address space, just like a process, but skip syscall overhead
It's slower because kernel threads always run at a lower CPU priority than user-level threads
mcqs.explanation: A kernel thread creation involves the kernel (a real cost a pure user-level thread avoids) but shares the process's existing address space rather than building a new one (the expensive part of process creation) — landing it in between the two in cost. Priority isn't the mechanism here.

mcqs.question: In a many-to-one threading model, one of five user-level threads makes a blocking disk read syscall. What happens to the other four?
options: They keep running normally on other CPU cores
They all freeze too, because the kernel sees only a single kernel thread and that one thread is now blocked
They're automatically promoted to their own kernel threads to keep running
Only the two threads created most recently are affected
mcqs.explanation: Many-to-one maps all user-level threads onto one kernel thread; the kernel has no visibility into the other four, so when the single kernel thread blocks, none of them can run — this is the model's defining flaw. There's no automatic promotion, and it isn't about which threads are 'recent.'

mcqs.question: How do Go's goroutines avoid the classic many-to-one blocking problem while still being much cheaper than OS threads?
options: Every goroutine is actually a full one-to-one OS thread under the hood, just renamed
Goroutines never perform blocking operations, so the problem never arises
The runtime multiplexes many goroutines over a small pool of real OS threads (many-to-many), and parks a goroutine that would block while moving its OS thread on to run others
Goroutines run only on a single OS thread total, accepting the many-to-one trade-off deliberately
mcqs.explanation: Go's runtime uses a many-to-many model: a pool of OS threads (sized by GOMAXPROCS) runs many lightweight goroutines, and when one would block, the runtime detaches it from its OS thread so that thread can run other goroutines — avoiding both the all-or-nothing freeze and the cost of one OS thread per goroutine.

mcqs.question: Why did general-purpose operating systems like Linux and Windows settle on one-to-one threading as the default, rather than many-to-one or many-to-many?
options: Because syscalls became free to make on modern CPUs, eliminating the cost difference

Many-to-one's all-or-nothing blocking became unacceptable once multi-core machines were standard (it also can't use more than one core), and one-to-one's per-thread syscall cost was an acceptable trade for real parallelism and no shared blocking
Because many-to-many is impossible to implement correctly in a general-purpose kernel
Because kernel-level threads use less memory than user-level threads in every case
mcqs.explanation: The rise of multi-core hardware made many-to-one's single-core ceiling and one-blocks-all failure mode unacceptable, while one-to-one's higher per-thread syscall cost became a reasonable price for true parallelism and per-thread blocking isolation. Many-to-many is implementable (Go/Erlang prove it) but needs a sophisticated runtime scheduler most general OSes didn't build in by default.
